content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a framework to learn a classifier from data where input observations are given as intervals. The problem is mapped to a classical learning problem where the task is to find a function from the spaces of all intervals to a space of K scoring functions. Some generalisation bounds are then given, and a learning method inspired from multi-view approaches is proposed to solve the problem. The method is tested both on synthetic data sets and on a real world data set called mushroom.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+: an interesting problem, which is the one of learning from interval-valued or uncertain data
+: some results on generalisation bounds a bout the problem

-: the fact that the nature of the interval-valued data is not really discussed, and rather eluded by the authors. For instance, Hullermeier (in "Learning from Imprecise and Fuzzy Observations: Data Disambiguation through Generalized Loss Minimization") discusses some general strategies to learn from interval-valued data, and it would be necessary to have a positioning of the authors with respect to this kind of literature. Similarly, I would disagree with Remark 2 that the analysis done in super-set learning would not apply here. The discussion by Liu and Diettrich is rather theoretical, and having scenarios in which the perfect true value is inaccessible does not preclude from addressing the problem from a theoretical perspective (i.e. under which assumption is the underlying precise problem learnable at all). 

-: Section 3.2. is quite hard to follow for someone not very familiar with multi-view approaches. A bit more intuition or explanation would have been nice, although I do not know if that is possible. This is also true for Figure and Algorithm 1, and to be honest I cannot say that I fully followed them. Being unfamiliar with multi-view approaches, it is hard for me to provide ways in which the algorithm can be made simpler. 

-: in Section 4, there are just not enough details (in the main paper) to reproduce the method, and one could question why this particular choice of fuzzy transformation/membership functions? Why not taking regularly sampled values from intervals? Is there something special about those fuzzy transformation? While the previous steps have been motivated by the authors on theoretical basis, this step seems to a large extent ad-hoc, and no specific reason to use such convoluted tools is presented. 

-: Similarly, I was not able to completely follow the reasoning of the authors for the synthetic data generation. Why choosing such intervals for a_{ij} and b_{ij}? Why not simply drawing two numbers a,b from the same distribution (say uniform between 0 and 10) and taking [x-a,x+b] for the corresponding interval? From figure 2, it seems that looking at the lower-right bound of blue class and upper-left bound of the red class is sufficient to find a linear separator. Given that in the multi-view decomposition such bounds are taken, the problem does not appear really difficult from an interval perspective. The fact that intervals overlap does not prevent from having a clear structure here, and one may wonder if this is not the case in other experiments.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4H3Z (3/4)
content.comment:
Comments 3:  In Section 4, there are just not enough details (in the main paper) to reproduce the method, and one could question why this particular choice of fuzzy transformation/membership functions? Why not taking regularly sampled values from intervals? Is there something special about those fuzzy transformation? While the previous steps have been motivated by the authors on theoretical basis, this step seems to a large extent ad-hoc, and no specific reason to use such convoluted tools is presented.

Response 3: Thank you for your valuable comments. We summarize your comments and your main question are: 1. what the motivation for choosing fuzzy transformation/membership functions; 2. why not take regularly sampled values from intervals. We will address your questions one by one.

First, The interval-valued features contain similar structures and properties with fuzzy numbers, which both exist a considerable amount of uncertainty. A fuzzy number is a generalization of a regular, real number in the sense that it does not refer to one single value but rather to a connected set of possible values, where each possible value has its own weight between 0 and 1. This weight is called the membership function. A fuzzy number is thus a special case of a convex, normalized fuzzy set of the real line. Particular cases include usual real numbers and intervals. Further, the $\alpha$-cut of a fuzzy number $\widetilde{x}$ is defined as {$t\in\mathbb{R}|\mu_{\widetilde{x}}(t)\leq\alpha$} ($\mu_{\widetilde{x}}(t)$ is the membership function of $\widetilde{x}$), which is a closed and bounded interval. Therefore, we design two fuzzilization methods to transfer the interval-valued features into two well-defined fuzzy numbers, which are triangular fuzzy number and Gaussian fuzzy number. 

Moreover, the four membership function-based methods can extract different crucial discriminant information from fuzzy numbers. More details analysis are shown as follow:

>The MOM method which selects a nonfuzzy output value corresponding to the maximum value of the membership function. When there is more than one such output value, the values are averaged. MOM finds the maximum membership level but ignores the changing trend of the membership function. 

>COG takes into account the trend and finds the centroid of the area bounded by the membership function. 

>ALC is flat averaging of all midpoints of the $\alpha$-cut, i.e., without weighting. The ALC is also equivalent to calculate the Expected Value (EV) of a fuzzy number.

>VAL uses $\alpha$-cut as weighting factors in averaging the $\alpha$-cut midpoints. VAL is intuitive to consider the individual contributions of each $\alpha$-cut, in which the $x$ values that appear in more $\alpha$-cut should have a greater contribution in defuzzification than the others.

Based on the above analysis, it inspired us to construct a set of transformation functions by fusing the two fuzzilization methods and the four membership function-based methods to extract multi-view discriminant information. Experimental results shown in Sections 5.2 and 5.3 verify the rationality and efficacy of these transformation functions.

In the revision, we add one paragraph to clearly introduce the motivation of transformation functions construction in Section 4 (see the second highlighted part on page 5 of the revised version).

For your second question, taking regularly sampled values from intervals can only extract single-view information, which may miss some crucial discriminant information. Further, we add three additional weak baselines called L-IIE, U-IIE and M-IIE that take the low bound, upper bound and midpoint values from intervals (i.e., take regularly sampled values from intervals) to train classifiers to compare with our method. The results from the following Table show our method outperforms all these three baselines in both synthetics and real-world datasets (see pages 7 and 8 of the revised version).

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4H3Z (2/4)
content.comment:
Commets 2: Section 3.2. is quite hard to follow for someone not very familiar with multi-view approaches. A bit more intuition or explanation would have been nice, although I do not know if that is possible. This is also true for Figure and Algorithm 1, and to be honest I cannot say that I fully followed them. Being unfamiliar with multi-view approaches, it is hard for me to provide ways in which the algorithm can be made simpler.

Response 2: Thank you for your valuable comments. 

First, we give a brief introduction of multi-view learning. Multi-view learning is an emerging direction in machine learning that aims to learn one function to model each view and jointly optimizes all the functions to improve the generalization performance. Multi-view learning is also known as data fusion or integration of data from multiple feature sets.  Moreover, multi-view data are very common in real world applications. Many data are often collected from different measuring methods as particular single-view data cannot comprehensively describe the information of all examples. For instance, for images and videos, color information and texture information are two different kinds of features, which can be regarded as two-view data. 

In this paper, we consider applying multi-view learning to analyze interval-valued data because interval-valued data exist a considerable amount of uncertainty. The existing single-view methods (like DF-SVM and DF-MLP) only extract single-view discriminant information from interval-valued data to train classifiers and can not reasonably handle this uncertainty. While our proposed model can extract multi-view discriminant information and use the extracted multi-view discriminant information to train multi-view classifiers, which can largely resolve this uncertainty.

In the revision, to make the reader easier to follow our theory and methods, we only introduce one main theoretical outcome (Theorem 1) and briefly summarize the analytical results and purpose of other theories in the main text. All proof and further theoretical analysis are moved in the Appendix B.2 (see the highlighted part on pages 18 and 21 of the revised version). The briefly summarize is shown as follow.

>"In addition, we prove two theorems (See Appendix B.2 for details) to illustrate the advantage of using multi-view learning to address the LIND problem in terms of error rate and estimation error bound. Theorem 4 shows that the error rate of a multi-view prediction function is lower than that of any single-view prediction function under some certain restrictions, which means that using multi-view methodology can reduce the error rate of the predict function for the classification tasks. Theorem 5 demonstrates that we can obtain tighter estimation error bound by applying the multi-view methodology. Inspired by the theoretical analysis of Theorems 4 and 5, we decide to find appropriate multi-view features that can achieve well and similar performance on some specific classifiers to train our multi-view classifiers.'' (see the first highlighted part on pages 3 and 4 of the revised version)

Furthermore, we redesigned Figure 1 to well-illustrate how to choose the candidate views and how to use the candidate views to get the view fusion representation vectors (see page 4 of the revised version). We rewrote Algorithm 1 to make it more precise and easy to follow, even if you are unfamiliar with multi-view approaches (see the first highlighted part on page 5 of the revised version).

We thank Reviewer 4H3Z for helpful feedback to improve our work. In this paper, we focus on constructing a new model via multi-view learning to address interval-valued data classification problems. We first identify the proposed problem called LINO and prove one theorem to demonstrate that we can always well handle the LIND problem when enough interval-valued instances can be collected.

In addition, we present two theorems to show the advantage of multi-view learning. Theorem 4 (in revision) shows that the error rate of a multi-view prediction function is lower than that of any single-view prediction function under some certain restrictions, which means that using multi-view methodology can reduce the error rate of the predict function for the classification tasks. Theorem 5 (in revision) demonstrates that we can obtain tighter estimation error bounds by applying the multi-view methodology. 

Further, the experiment results on both synthetic and real-world datasets verify the superiority and rationality of applying multi-view methodology to address the proposed problem.

Point-by-point responses to some of your questions are listed below.

Comments 1: The fact that the nature of the interval-valued data is not really discussed, and rather eluded by the authors. For instance, Hullermeier (in "Learning from Imprecise and Fuzzy Observations: Data Disambiguation through Generalized Loss Minimization") discusses some general strategies to learn from interval-valued data, and it would be necessary to have a positioning of the authors with respect to this kind of literature. Similarly, I would disagree with Remark 2 that the analysis done in super-set learning would not apply here. The discussion by Liu and Diettrich is rather theoretical, and having scenarios in which the perfect true value is inaccessible does not preclude from addressing the problem from a theoretical perspective (i.e. under which assumption is the underlying precise problem learnable at all).

Response 1: Thank you for your valuable comments. The problem under which assumption is the underlying precise problem learnable is significant. In future work, we will focus on addressing this problem and further discuss the nature of the interval-valued data. However, in this paper, we mainly focus on designing a well-performed machine-learning model to address a more realistic problem of interval-valued real-world data classification. In addition, we detail an application of our proposed method in that we present a novel framework for protecting data privacy. 

Besides, we discuss the contribution of the paper (Learning from Imprecise and Fuzzy Observations: Data Disambiguation through Generalized Loss Minimization) in imprecise data analysis and cite it in our paper.

>"Recently, some researchers have begun exploring imprecise data from different perspectives, such as superset label learning and data disambiguation (Cour et al. content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of classification from features which are of interval type, as opposed to features which have precise or “crisp” values. To solve this problem, an interval is transformed into a seven values, next fed to a multiview classifier which produces and fuses candidate views and produces final classification. Theoretical result on estimation error bound, based on the empirical Rademacher complexity, was presented. The approach was evaluated on synthetic and real data and application to data privacy protection was illustrated.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
Theoretical treatment was performed thoroughly and presented in great detail.
Application within the privacy-preserving framework is quite novel and interesting.

Weaknesses:
It is suggested that interval valued data are “common”, but I would argue that they are rather “uncommon”. The example brought up is of a mushroom dataset (table 1.), where certain diameters/lengths are presented as intervals. While those intervals are describing ranges for certain mushroom species, a single mushroom specimen would still have a crisp value measurement. Also, examples of measurement instruments which are returning intervals could have been mentioned.

I acknowledge that multi-view architecture was suggested by theoretical findings that “view-invariant” features have tighter error bounds, but would still be curious to see its effect on empirical performance. Ablation study was mentioned, but there is no appendix where it is supposed to be found. I feel that there should be space for such results of an ablation study in the main part of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The approach appears novel, but evaluation quality could be improved with more baselines, like for example classifiers proposed specifically for interval data type, eg (Utkin & Coolen, 2011) . Problem definition is clear, proposed methodology is also clear, and code and data is promised to be shared, which should make the presented results reproducible. 
Overall well written, except that abbreviations are not defined like DF-SVM, etc. And table 1. mentions row 2-6 but table has just 5 rows.
content.summary_of_the_review: Having stated perceived shortcomings on the necessity of the approach - overly complex without ablation support, and insufficient empirical evaluation against the weak baselines - no other competing approach specifically tailored for interval data, I am leaning more towards the rejection.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.comment: Thanks to authors for pointing to my overlook of the Ablation study results in the Appendix, as well as for accepting suggestion and adding it to the main text of the paper. content.summary_of_the_paper:
Interval data is a frequently used data type in our daily life. However, the reverent machine learning or deep learning studies are rare. In this paper, the authors did the first study regarding the Learning from Interval-valued Data, which is very significant at the first glance. In addition, this paper provides a very interesting application to use the proposed algorithm: using interval data to protect the data privacy, which is direct and promising application in the real world.

As for the technical part, this paper gives the first learning bound regarding the interval-valued data, which is a good start for this problem, especially in the field of machine learning. Then, this paper proposes a promising algorithm based on the theory and deep learning. In the end, the proposed algorithm is validated by the synthetic data and the real-world data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

1.  The problem setting is very important, filling up a gap between machine learning theory/algorithm between interval-valued data type that is a frequently used data type in the real world but is neglected by the machine learning community.

2. The proposed theory is important to this new problem setting and supports the design of the proposed algorithm. 

3. Applying the intervalization procedure to real data to protect data privacy is very interesting. This way seems direct and promising. Because we actually cannot convert the interval data back, which directly keep original data safe.

4. It is a big plus to find real datasets and verify the proposed algorithm on the real datasets. When comparing the results, the statistical testing is performed to ensure the improvement is significantly in the view of statistics.

Cons:

1. In section 4, seven ways are selected to transform the data. Why do you choose these ways? A clear justification is required here.

2. Algorithm 1 is quite dense. Separating steps could be better for readers.

3. It is interesting to see that DF-MLP does not perform well on the mushroom dataset. More intuition behind its failure should be analysed, because they are common solution to the interval valued data-based machine learning algorithms.

4. The motivation to use EN is not clear in section 5.4. It is from other papers or proposed in this paper? More explanations should be added in this part.

5. What is the difference between differential privacy and your methods in the data-privacy part? Please explicitly list common and different aspects between both.

6. In Figure 1, it is difficult to see the connect between candidate views and view fusion. In addition, candidate views are output from y? In my opinion, Figure 1 should be reworked.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mFK1 (2/2)
content.comment:
Comment 5: What is the difference between differential privacy and your methods in the data-privacy part? Please explicitly list common and different aspects between both.

Response 5: Thank you for your valuable comment. A discussion of common and different aspects between differential privacy and our methods is given in Section 5.4. See the following description.

>"Differential privacy (DP) and homomorphic encryption are common used schemes to achieve privacy-preserving. DP and homomorphic encryption can be applied to the raw data or the algorithm, but our method only applies to the raw data. DP applied to the raw data is based on data-perturbation, and homomorphic encryption is based on data-encryption, but the amount of data is not changed. Moreover, if the keys of the encryption schemes are compromised, the information of the raw data will also be compromised. While our method compresses the raw data into interval-valued data with fewer instances through an irreversible process to protect data privacy. Further, DP and our approach can not be easily applied to image data, which is a meaningful problem worth considering in the future.''(see the second highlighted part on page 9 of the revised version)

Comment 6: In Figure 1, it is difficult to see the connection between candidate views and view fusion. In addition, candidate views are output from y? In my opinion, Figure 1 should be reworked.

Response 6: Thank you for your valuable comment.  In our model, candidate views are selected on the validation set that achieves higher classification accuracy than the rest of the views. We redesigned Figure 1 to well-illustrate how to choose the candidate views and how to use the candidate views to get the view fusion representation vectors (see page 4 of the revised version).

Comment 7: Since we might only have a few interval-valued data, how could you ensure that the optimized solution can be obtained due to the theory.

Response 7: This question is important. In the future study, we will consider applying other techniques, for example, meta-learning, to address interval-valued data classification problems with few data.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mFK1 (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer mFK1 for positive comments and helpful feedback to improve our paper. Point-by-point responses to your comments are listed below.

Comment 1: In section 4, seven ways are selected to transform the data. Why do you choose these ways? A clear justification is required here.

Response 1: Thank you for your crucial comment. The motivation for transformation functions construction is discussed as follow:

The interval-valued features contain similar structures and properties with fuzzy numbers, which both exist a considerable amount of uncertainty. A fuzzy number is a generalization of a regular, real number in the sense that it does not refer to one single value but rather to a connected set of possible values, where each possible value has its own weight between 0 and 1. This weight is called the membership function. A fuzzy number is thus a special case of a convex, normalized fuzzy set of the real line. Particular cases include usual real numbers and intervals. Further, the $\alpha$-cut of a fuzzy number $\widetilde{x}$ is defined as {$t\in\mathbb{R}|\mu_{\widetilde{x}}(t)\leq\alpha$} ($\mu_{\widetilde{x}}(t)$ is the membership function of $\widetilde{x}$), which is a closed and bounded interval. Therefore, we design two fuzzilization methods to transfer the interval-valued features into two well-defined fuzzy numbers, which are triangular fuzzy number and Gaussian fuzzy number. 

Moreover, the four membership function-based methods can extract different crucial discriminant information from fuzzy numbers. More details analysis are shown as follow:

>The MOM method which selects a nonfuzzy output value corresponding to the maximum value of the membership function. When there is more than one such output value, the values are averaged. MOM finds the maximum membership level but ignores the changing trend of the membership function. 

>COG takes into account the trend and finds the centroid of the area bounded by the membership function. 

>ALC is flat averaging of all midpoints of the $\alpha$-cut, i.e., without weighting. The ALC is also equivalent to calculate the Expected Value (EV) of a fuzzy number.

>VAL uses $\alpha$-cut as weighting factors in averaging the $\alpha$-cut midpoints. VAL is intuitive to consider the individual contributions of each $\alpha$-cut, in which the $x$ values that appear in more $\alpha$-cut should have a greater contribution in defuzzification than the others.

Based on the above analysis, it inspired us to construct a set of transformation functions by fusing the two fuzzilization methods and the four membership function-based methods to extract multi-view discriminant information.

We add one paragraph to clearly introduce the motivation of transformation functions construction in Section 4 (see the second highlighted part on page 5 of the revised version).

Comment 2: Algorithm 1 is quite dense. Separating steps could be better for readers.

Response 2: Thank you for your lovely comment. We rewrote Algorithm 1 to make it more precise and easy to follow (see the first highlighted part on page 5 of the revised version).

Comment 3: More intuition behind its failure should be analysed.

Response 3: Thank you for your nice comment. To address this we added the following sentence to give a further analysis of the failure of DF-MLP and DF-SVM on the mushroom dataset:

>"DF-SVM and DF-MLP perform much worse than our methods on the mushroom dataset because they ignore some crucial discriminant information from this dataset. In comparison, our methods via multi-view learning and fuzzy transformation functions can extract more discriminant information.''(see the second highlighted part on page 8 of the revised version)

Comment 4: The motivation to use EN is not clear in section 5.4. 

Response 4: Thank you for your valuable comment. EN is proposed in this paper. We give a further introduction and analysis of EN in Section 5.4.

>"We define EN=1-(m+n*q)/n, where (m+n*q) is the amount of data that the computation party can receive from the data owner(s) and n is the amount of raw data. A smaller EN means the computation party will receive more data from the data owner(s), so the computation party may receive more information about the raw data. Therefore, EN can be used to measure the degree of privacy-preserving by applying INPP. Greater EN means greater privacy protection by applying INPP.''(see the first highlighted part on page 9 of the revised version)

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper proposes a multiview deep learning approach to learn from interval-valued data, i.e. data that do not come as crisp numbers but rather as interval. Rademacher complexity based results on the generalization property of models learned on such interval data are provided, together with extensive numerical simulations showing the relevance of the proposed learning architecture.

Strengths:
- learning from interval-valued data might become key
- there is a connection with privacy-preserving machine learning that is outlined
- there is a deep learning architecture proposed to learn from interval valued data

Weaknesses:
- a better motivation / accounting on the ubiquitousness of interval valued data could be provided
- as outlined by Reviewer 4H3Z, there are many parts (section 3, section 4) that lack the necessary detail for the reader to fully grasp what is depicted; it is as thought the authors only give "previews" of the results, without the necessary motivations, the right keys to read and ingest the results;
- more generally, the authors could have made a (lot) better choice at selecting what they wanted to say: there are many many many results presented here, not with much connectedness (e.g. is the thing about privacy key or not to the approach here?) and with an hard-to-follow break down as to why such part is in the appendix and this other is not. 

One of the reviewers suggested to go for a journal publication to have the opportunity not to choose between the various contributions: I would say that the challenge is bigger than putting everything in a paper, it is rather to build the right logical and compelling connection between all the parts which, as of now, struggle to blend together.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The take-home message of what is done here is not clear. Too much and diverse information.
content.justification_for_why_not_lower_score: The topic of learning from interval valued data may be interesting.
